newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends quiet US session higher, eyes Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends quiet US session higher, eyes Greenspan.

text.p: The dollar ended an extremely thin U.S. session marginally higher, reaping modest gains from a French audit of public finances, but sticking to recent ranges ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
For the first time in five trading sessions, the greenback failed to hurdle the 1.80 mark level, but dealers said the U.S. currency was well supported and predicted more strength in the days to come.

"The closes, week to week, have been higher for dollar/mark, so if you look from a medium-term perspective it's still got a channel line pointing higher," said Steven Jonathan, director, foreign exchange at Merrill Lynch.
The dollar ended at 1.7960/70 marks, up from 1.7930/40 at the open. It also rose to 116.10/20 yen from 115.85/90.

As expected, the French audit revealed on Monday that the country's budget deficit was running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product for 1997 -- well above the 3.0 percent target mandated by the Maastricht treaty for countries launching the single currency in 1999.
The French government announced it would raise taxes on big business and cut spending in order to reduce the deficit ratio and get closer to the 3.0 percent goal.
The fiscal measures fuelled expectations that Europe's currency plan would go ahead on schedule, but raised fears that the euro would be a weak, broad-based unit.

"If you look at the French audit it still appears that the euro is going to be a weak currency and I think that's the reason the dollar came back," said Rob Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke reinforced these expectations when he said he expected a timely start to monetary union, including both France and Germany, despite the French government's inability to meet the 3.0 percent target.

And Welteke's colleague Hans-Juergen Krupp, also speaking on Monday, said worries that the euro would be an unstable currency if all countries did not meet the 3.0 percent deficit/GDP target were unfounded.
On a day when activity in the major currencies was extremely light, the Indonesian rupiah fell victim to bouts of speculative selling overseas, lending dollar/yen a modest bid, dealers said.

Speculative selling has battered the Thai baht, Philippine peso, Malaysian ringgit and Singapore dollar in recent weeks and dealers said the rupiah's fall represented spillover from the markets of Indonesia's Southeast Asian neighbors.

The Sea's Day holiday in Japan and caution ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress, to be delivered on Tuesday and Wednesday, contributed to subdued trading, dealers said.
"We have Greenspan coming up and Japan was out on holiday which gives people an excuse to sit back and watch from the sidelines," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank New York.
In other trading on Monday, the dollar ended lower at 1.4755/65 Swiss francs against 1.4762/72 at the open, and higher at Canadian $1.3772/77 versus C$1.3730/35.
The British pound climbed to $1.6782/92 against $1.6752/62, while the Australian dollar edged down to close at $0.7407/12 from $0.7414/19.
